title: The invitation to try out for Chautauqua
summary: In his last year of high school, Dorothy Green and a violinist take him to Chicago to audition for Chautauqua as a novelty xylophone soloist, with his mother's encouragement.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: So then, in my last year in high school this Dorothy Green down the street and another girl were going to Chicago to try out for Chataqua, which was a tent thing, and it happened in all the small towns in the Midwest in those days, I don't know if you ever heard about it. It was like Lyceum and like I seen them in Chataqua, in the wintertime it was Lyceum, Beards-town and they'd have -- they'd come into, say, Georgetown, they'd put up a tent in one of the school yards.
And they'd have lectures, they'd have oh, different musical things. Oh, maybe a string quartet one afternoon, and something else --
-- and they have tickets you buy by the Chamber of Commerce, and everybody in town would go they'd by a weekly ticket.

They'd have a program layed and out. So this is the sort of thing -- the one girl had been in Chataqua before. So, they inveigled me to go up with them. So -- well I can't read, I thought what am I gonna -- so they said, you play. And I was playing a few solos, back in high school, at that time in assemblies --

So they said come on up, why not. So my mother said, what have you got to lose, you're going to the University of Illinois in the Fall, mean, go on up, you can travel for nothing. I used to travel on the railroad cause my father was a railroader, for nothing.
I see, so the people that were in it, were they employed in it?
No, no. She was still in high -- my gade in high school. She was just going up with this other girl who was a concert violinist -- see?
So they took me along as a -- like a novelty thing, see?
And I played a couple of solos --
I don't remember what it was, I don't remember what they were now.
I think that's about four or five things is all I knew.
Yeah. Could you read music then?
No, I couldn't read music. I knew what the notes were --
When you say read, I mean I knew the notes --
-- I knew the keys and all that sort of thing --
But I mean to -- to be a fast reader, like you'd have to to be a professional --
